Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Search and rescue operations continue after the Filo Jet, a high-speed passenger ferry, sank on Sunday near Kyrenia. Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images Cyprus Turkish deep-sea search vessel joins efforts to retrieve 20 still missing after Cyprus ferry disaster TCG Isin expected to play vital role in locating Filo Jet’s voyage data recorder 514 metres below surface Helena Smith in Athens Mon 31 Aug 2026 14.37 EDT Last modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 15.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A deep-sea search and rescue vessel is on its way to Cyprus as Turkey joins efforts to retrieve the 20 people still missing after a passenger ferry capsized off the island’s northern coast. The TCG Isin will join the vast operation to find survivors after the high-speed ferry sank on Sunday barely four nautical miles outside the port town of Kyrenia. Authorities confirmed late on Monday – the first of three days of national mourning in Turkish-held northern Cyprus – that the tragedy had claimed eight lives , increasing the number of passengers still unaccounted for from 17 to 20. A total of 241 of the 267 people aboard the Filo Jet, bound for Taşucu on the Turkish mainland when it began to take on water, had been rescued, they said. Almost all were either Turkish or Turkish Cypriot. Nearly 20 people still missing after ferry capsizes ⁠off northern Cyprus Read more View image in fullscreen Survivors arrive on shore. Of the 267 people on board the ferry, 241 have been rescued, authorities have said. Photograph: Reuters International sympathy for the victims was highlighted as the Anglo-Cypriot founder of easyJet, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, offered €260,000 (£223,000) in support for the families of the deceased and missing, in a move hailed by Turkish Cypriot officials. Visiting Kyrenia’s new port, where relatives gathered for news of loved ones on Monday, Tufan Erhürman , the self-styled state’s president, vowed search efforts would “continue with the same intensity, with no interruption, through the day and night”. The Isin , capable of searching up to 3,000 metres below the sea surface, was due to arrive on Tuesday, he said, as he comforted the families of those still missing. The ship is expected to play a vital role in recovering the ferry’s voyage data recorder, or black box, now viewed as key in deciphering the cause of a maritime disaster not seen since the breakaway territory declared independence in 1983. Turkish Cypriot officials told the Guardian it was likely “all those responsible” would be charged with gross negligence as the seaworthiness of the 26-year-old ferry was also questioned. The owners and shareholders of the privately owned company operating the passenger vessel have also been ordered to appear in court. View image in fullscreen The Turkish Cypriot leader, Tufan Erhürman, talks with relatives waiting for news outside the port of Kyrenia. Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/Reuters It remained unclear whether those still missing had been trapped on board. “Nobody is saying it publicly, but the hope of any survivors being found at this point is very slim,” one official confided. “Those who weren’t rescued very likely didn’t find a lifejacket. We believe many were elderly people and mothers with babies and young kids.” In testimony – and video footage – that emerged on Monday, panic-stricken passengers could be seen desperately looking for lifejackets and screaming before the double-hulled ferry flipped over. One mother, Ayten Biçer, described feeling her 12-year-old daughter slip from her hands and disappear as the ferry capsized and sank in a matter of minutes. “She was saying, ‘Don’t let go.’ And I didn’t let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn’t let her go,” she sobbed. Two of Biçer’s other children are among the 20 still missing. View image in fullscreen Ayten and Hayri Biçer wait for news of their two missing children outside the port of Kyrenia. Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/Reuters The captain of the ferry and seven crew members were detained on Monday as judicial authorities launched an inquiry into the tragedy amid claims they had been among the first to abandon ship. Appearing before a local magistrate, the crew attributed the disaster to the bow of the catamaran-style ferry breaking apart in turbulent seas. But eyewitness accounts contradicted that version of events, with passengers telling officials that appeals to turn back to port had fallen on deaf ears as the ferry began to take on water. Ünal Üstel, the northern Cyprus prime minister, told reporters the Filo Jet was lying on the seabed at a depth of 514 metres and that he foresaw the Turkish salvage ship “reaching [it] tomorrow afternoon”. Boats, helicopters, aircraft and other search and rescue teams had joined the operation, he said, adding that search efforts were continuing “on a 24-hour basis”. Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when a coup aimed at union with Greece – engineered by the military junta then in power in Athens – prompted Turkey to invade and seize the island’s northern third. Ever since, as many as 45,000 mainland Turkish troops have been stationed in the north. In 1983, the territory unilaterally declared independence, but in the absence of a settlement, decades of international isolation have ensued. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PA View image in fullscreen The City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city. Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PA Extreme heat Cities in Great Britain most vulnerable to extreme heat revealed OS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperatures Sandra Laville Environment correspondent Mon 7 Sep 2026 19.01 EDT Last modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Portsmouth, Leicester, Exeter, Bristol and Nottingham will be among the cities that warm the most by the end of this century as global heating turns British cities into urban heat islands, according to research. Analysis from Ordnance Survey (OS) has created a heat vulnerability index for all cities in Great Britain. Portsmouth , which sits on the south coast of England and is home to 208,000 people, is the most vulnerable to extreme heat today and into the future, according to the research from the OS, the Met Office and the data analysis company 4 Earth Intelligence. Concrete, asphalt, buildings and hard surfaces in cities absorb solar radiation during the day and act like giant radiators, holding on to the heat rather than cooling down at night as in more rural areas. Cities can be up to 10C hotter than surrounding areas. Areas most at risk of extreme warming are those with the least tree cover , green space and waterways. View image in fullscreen Portsmouth is the most vulnerable to extreme heat today and into the future, according to the research. Photograph: Peter Titmuss/Alamy This summer was provisionally the UK’s hottest on record , and the research reveals which cities are suffering now from intense urban heat and which will be among the warmest in future. The research analyses 71 cities granted by royal charter across England, Scotland and Wales but excluding Northern Ireland. The OS heat vulnerability index suggests that by 2040 all 71 cities will reach high heat vulnerability. By the turn of the century, almost two-thirds could reach the most severe level. Those facing the most severe impact by the end of the century are predicted to be Portsmouth, the City of Westminster, Plymouth, Leicester and Exeter, according to the analysis. Nick Bolton, the chief executive of Ordnance Survey, said: “Cities are where millions of people live, work and spend their everyday lives. “Extreme and sustained heat can affect people’s health and wellbeing, how comfortable our homes and workplaces are, and put additional pressure on transport, energy and emergency services. Understanding how and where this vulnerability is changing depends on an accurate view of how the country is built, based on trusted authoritative data, which is critical for planners, developers and local authorities preparing for a warmer future.” UK ‘built for climate that no longer exists’ and needs urgent changes to survive global heating, report warns Read more Portsmouth is today the most heat-vulnerable city and will remain at the highest level for warming until the end of the century, according to the research. The city of Leicester is projected to show the biggest rise in Britain’s heat vulnerability rankings, climbing from 10th now to fourth by the end of the century, while Exeter and Nottingham also rise into the 10 most vulnerable cities, alongside Bristol and Brighton and Hove by the end of this century. Leaders in Portsmouth have identified areas including Somerstown, Portsea, Southsea and Fratton as those particularly exposed to urban heat because of their limited green areas and hard surfaces, and noted that areas with less green space overlap with those of deprivation. The City of London and the City of Westminster areas rank among the most heat-retentive urban environments in the UK. The City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city, given the concentration of buildings, roads and hard surfaces as well as limited green space, trees and water. Westminster ranks third for overall heat vulnerability today and second in both future periods behind Portsmouth. View image in fullscreen Tree cover, green space and waterways can help mitigate the effects of global heating. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian A study commissioned by the mayor of London has put the total economic cost of the 2022 London heatwaves at £1.5bn, including productivity losses, health impacts, education disruption, energy demand, transport and emergency services. The OS heat vulnerability index combined current observed temperatures with the structural characteristics of Britain’s built environment and climate projections into the future to produce a score for every city on a scale of 1 to 5, where 3 to 4 is high and 4 to 5 is severe. Among cities coping the best with the changing climate is Milton Keynes, which ranks 69th out of 71 cities for heat vulnerability today. Milton Keynes has the lowest built-environment vulnerability in England and the most effective natural cooling of any city in the analysis, with 46 sq km of natural surfaces, against almost 40 sq km of hard made surfaces. Jonathan Hendry, the chief executive of 4 Earth Intelligence, said exposure varied street by street within a single city. “The areas consistently subjected to higher temperatures than their surroundings are the ones that overheat first during a heatwave,” he said. “We’re mapping how to turn thermal threats into actionable blueprints for urban resilience, supporting decisions on where heat refuges are sited and how emergency responses are planned in advance rather than in the middle of climate events.” Explore more on these topics Extreme heat Climate crisis Portsmouth Construction industry The sun London Plymouth news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/27/pola.text: Poland and Lithuania are working on an international evacuation plan for civilians in the event of a major crisis or military threat.If necessary, the plan would allow some residents of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia to be moved across the Polish border.Vilmantas Vitkauskas, the head of Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre, has announced that work on the proposal was already under way and that representatives of Lithuania and Poland were analysing procedures, logistics, and infrastructure capacity.A detailed plan is to be drawn up once Poland and Lithuania reach an appropriate agreement.The preparations are being carried out as part of Lithuania's "Vyčio Skliautas 2026" exercises, launched on 25 September to test its national mobilisation system and institutional cooperation in a crisis situation.The drills will run until 3 October. One of their practical components is testing procedures for the evacuation of the population.Around 3,000 officials, officers, and representatives of institutions, local authorities, companies, and non-governmental organisations are taking part in the exercises, along with about 1,000 volunteers. A delegation of around 20 people from various Polish institutions has also arrived in Lithuania.During the drills, systems for warning residents, the organisation of assembly and registration points, transport, and the movement of evacuees through successive regions are being put to the test. Poland is also involved in work related to planning cross-border evacuation.The Lithuanian authorities have stressed that the aim of the exercises is to develop and test procedures for dealing with crises. The exercises are training activities and do not mean authorities are expecting an imminent threat.The Suwałki gapThe Suwałki gap, a strip of territory linking Poland and Lithuania - and therefore connecting the Baltic states with other NATO allies and the rest of the European Union - is of particular importance to the plan.The area contains the main land routes between Lithuania and Poland. In the event of a serious crisis, the region could prove to be crucial for the movement of troops and supplies as well as for the evacuation of civilians."The Suwałki gap is of huge importance, both militarily and logistically," Vitkauskas said.Poland prepares to receive evacueesPoland is also preparing for the possibility of receiving evacuees from the Baltic states.In September, representatives from Lithuania and Latvia visited Poland on a study trip focused, among other things, on mass evacuation, civil protection, and the organisation of reception and accommodation for evacuees.Talks were attended by representatives of Polish services and institutions responsible for security and civil protection.Lithuania has already drawn up its own evacuation plan for residents in the event of a military threat or crisis.One of the main evacuation routes runs from Vilnius towards the Polish border. Authorities in Poland's Podlaskie Voivodeship are preparing the region for a potential role as a transit corridor for residents of the Baltic states.

https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-annou.text: LONDON — The U.K. government is removing import tariffs on more than 100 products, including food, drink and fuel, to ease the cost of living. In a pre-budget announcement on Monday night, the Treasury said it would suspend tariffs on a number of popular food items, including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, as well as fertilizer and kerosene heating oil. The announcement, which follows a consultation earlier this year, comes after the government said last week that it would suspend import tariffs on over 250 goods that were due to expire on Dec. 31 until Dec. 2028. Advertisement Advertisement Collectively, the government said the tariff suspensions would reduce consumer costs by around £245 million to £595 million a year. “Today's everyday fixes are just a small part of what we are doing to give families a bit of breathing space,” Chancellor John Healey said. “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting families here at home through higher everyday costs. We can’t control global events, but we can act where we can make a difference.”

http://eng.chinamil.com.cn/2025xb/W/N/16.text: China Military HOME CHINA Featured Story Training & Exercise Exchange & Cooperation Military Operations Other Than War Law Enforcement VOICE OPINION WORLD World News Analysis MULTIMEDIA Photo Video European leaders question Trump's Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire This photo taken on Sept. 17, 2026 shows smoke rising after a drone and missile attack in Kiev, Ukraine. Twelve people were injured, including two children, in a Russian drone and missile attack on the Ukrainian capital early Thursday, said Kiev Mayor Vitali Klitschko. (Photo: Xinhua) European leaders on Monday questioned whether Russia would honor an "energy ceasefire" announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, while saying a real halt to attacks on energy infrastructure could offer relief if implemented. The announcement, which Moscow has yet to confirm, came amid growing concerns in Europe over Washington's recent diesel supply agreement with Russia and its implications for Western sanctions and transatlantic relations. European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire if it was observed, but questioned whether Russia would comply. "We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds. We have not yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," Kallas told reporters ahead of a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg. She said a ceasefire limited to oil refineries would disproportionately benefit Russia, which has far more refining facilities than Ukraine. "If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is by putting more pressure on Russia," Kallas said, calling on the United States to impose sanctions on Moscow. LEADERS QUESTION RUSSIA'S COMMITMENT French President Emmanuel Macron said Monday that he had seen no sign of an energy ceasefire on the Russian side, pointing to continued strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also expressed skepticism about the prospects for a ceasefire. At the Warsaw Security Forum, he said Russia had repeatedly rejected proposals for de-escalation. "Russia is not interested in a ceasefire, or in de-escalation or peace," Tusk said, adding that European countries should have no illusions about Moscow's intentions. Tusk also called for further strengthening sanctions against Russia. Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics said that there were currently no signs Russia was ready to end the conflict, as Russian President Vladimir Putin remained convinced he could achieve victory. Nevertheless, Rinkevics said that a U.S.-brokered energy ceasefire, if successfully implemented, would benefit all sides. Europe should continue providing military and financial assistance to Ukraine and help the country prepare for the coming winter, he added. Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik, however, welcomed the ceasefire. He described the announcement as an opportunity to restore dialogue and move toward peace, while accusing European officials of prolonging the conflict through continued military assistance to Ukraine. DIESEL AGREEMENT DRAWS CRITICISM European criticism also focused on Washington's agreement with Moscow on diesel supplies. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Monday that the U.S.-Russia diesel agreement was "out of the question" for Germany and Europe. Russia would only negotiate seriously under pressure, he said. Germany would maintain its sanctions against Moscow, and he called for tougher measures following continued Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Hanna Notte, director of the Eurasia Nonproliferation Program at the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies and a non-resident senior associate at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the latest developments were creating new tensions between Washington and Kyiv and further straining transatlantic relations. "Politically, Russia is really the beneficiary here," Notte said. She said the diesel agreement set a precedent allowing Moscow to conclude bilateral economic deals with Washington without first reaching a settlement on the Ukraine conflict. It could also undermine the credibility of Western sanctions, particularly after years of efforts to discourage other countries from purchasing Russian energy, she argued. Felix Klauser, head of German public broadcaster ZDF's Moscow bureau, said the diesel agreement represented a political gain for the Kremlin, which could portray the easing of sanctions as a symbolic breakthrough at home and abroad. He said the agreement meanwhile increased pressure on Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian oil infrastructure. Its political symbolism appeared to matter more to Trump than the actual volume of Russian diesel reaching global markets before the U.S. midterm elections, Klauser said. QUESTIONS OVER CEASEFIRE TERMS Finnish national broadcaster Yle also raised questions about whether the proposed energy ceasefire would impose equal obligations on Russia and Ukraine. Markku Kangaspuro, a professor at the University of Helsinki, told Yle that Russia could benefit from the arrangement without even agreeing to a ceasefire. Tyyne Karjalainen, a researcher at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs, said that Ukraine could face more severe consequences if the ceasefire broke down, including the risk of Washington withdrawing security support. A commentary published Monday in The Irish Times argued that Trump's proposed energy ceasefire was heavily tilted in Russia's favor, potentially depriving Ukraine of one of its most effective means of exerting pressure on Moscow. Nevertheless, the commentary noted that expanding the ceasefire from oil refineries to all energy infrastructure could help ease Ukrainian civilians' suffering during the approaching winter. Such a move could pave the way for a broader ceasefire, it suggested, although a negotiated settlement to the conflict remained a distant prospect. Related News

https://hvg.hu/vilag/20261113_oroszok-na.text: Az oroszok azt is követelik, hogy a NATO ürítse ki a baltikumi bázisait, és Moldovát is szövetségi állammá akarnák alakítani. Az orosz tárgyalók az ukrajnai háború befejezéséről szóló abu-dzabi tárgyalások során súlyos követeléseket terjesztettek elő, többek között azt, hogy Finnország lépjen ki a NATO-ból, valamint hogy tiltsák meg a NATO-nak, hogy katonai támaszpontokat létesítsen a balti államokban – számolt be pénteken a Bild . A német napilap értesülései szerint az európaiakkal megosztott, informális javaslatok lényegesen túlmutatnak az ukrajnai háború rendezésén és egy új európai biztonsági berendezkedés kialakítását célozták meg. Az oroszok többek között továbbra is azt – az egyébként ezerszer cáfolt, lásd pl. itt és itt – a sérelmüket hangoztatják, hogy a nyugati kormányok megígérték nekik, hogy a NATO-t nem bővítik keleti irányban. A háború befejezésének feltételeként az oroszok megtartanák az általuk megszállt összes ukrán területet, és megkapnák mellé még a Donbasz ukrán kézen lévő maradékát. Odessza és Mikloajiv kikötőit demilitarizálnia kellene Kijevnek. Az ukrán NATO-tagságról szó sem lehet, maximum az Európai Unióhoz való csatlakozásról lehet majd egyszer beszélni. Az oroszoknak Moldovával is terveik vannak, az országot szövetségi alapon szerveznék újra, és a jelenleg szakadár orosz kamuállamként működő Transznisztria és Gagauzia is önálló egységekké válnának. Mindezért az oroszok annyit ajánlanának fel cserébe, hogy kivonják a nukleáris fegyvereiket Belaruszból. A mostani beszámoló azért is meglepő, mert az eddigi hírek éppen arról szóltak, hogy közelednek egymáshoz az álláspontok a tárgyalásokon, még az ukrán delegáció egyik tagja, a kormánypárt frakcióvezetője, David Arahamija is optimista hangot ütött meg . Ehhez képest a fenti orosz követelések kifejezetten szélsőségesek, még Moszkva korábbi álláspontjaihoz képest is. A finnek részéről az értesülésre reagálva Antti Häkkänen finn védelmi miniszter közölte, hogy Finnország NATO-tagsága nem képezheti semmiféle alku tárgyát. „Maga a felvetés is felháborító” – jelentette ki a Helsinki Times beszámolója szerint. „Erről én nem tudok. Ilyen nem volt. Egész biztos, hogy erről szó sem volt” – kommentálta a történteket Dmitrij Peszkov orosz elnöki szóvivő az RBC-nek nyilatkozva. Ugyanakkor a mostani tárgyalásokat összegezve Jurij Usakov, Vlagyimir Putyin tanácsadója csütörtökön arról beszélt , hogy ki kell alakítani egy új, posztháborús európai biztonsági rendet, mert a mostani láthatóan nem működik. Usakov arról is beszélt, hogy ennek az új rendnek a tartópilléreit azok a követelések képezik, amelyeket 2021-ben már megfogalmaztak. Ennek pedig részét képezte, hogy a NATO vonuljon vissza az 1997-es határaira, de hogy félreértés ne legyen, Usakov maga is külön kitért rá. A találkozó azonban egyelőre nem jött össze, mivel a neki szánt csomagot otthon hagyták, ezért vissza kellett menniük Székesfehérvárra. Első látásra semmi gyanús nem volt a hagyományos indiai édességben.
